cards.front: A full turn is [ ___ ]; a straight line is [ ___ ].
cards.back: A full turn is 360°; a straight line is 180°.

options.text: A full turn is 360°; a straight line is 180°.
options.explanation: One complete rotation returns to the starting direction and measures 360°, while the angle formed by a straight line is half a turn, measuring 180°.

options.text: A full turn is 180°; a straight line is 360°.
options.explanation: This reverses the two standard angle facts. A full turn measures 360°, whereas a straight line represents half a turn and measures 180°.

options.text: A full turn is 360°; a straight line is 90°.
options.explanation: A 90° angle is a quarter turn, not a straight line. A full turn measures 360°, and a straight line measures 180°.

options.text: A full turn is 180°; a straight line is 90°.
options.explanation: This confuses a half turn with a full turn and a quarter turn with a straight line. The correct measures are 360° and 180°, respectively.

cards.front: What do angles in a triangle add up to?

options.explanation: The three interior angles of any triangle have a total of 180°, regardless of the triangle’s side lengths or individual angle sizes.
A total of 360° applies to angles around a point or the interior angles of a quadrilateral. The angles inside a triangle add to 180°.
A right angle measures 90°, but that is not the total for every triangle. The three interior angles of a triangle add to 180°.
A total of 270° may result from confusing three right angles with a triangle’s angle sum. Every triangle’s interior angles instead total 180°.

cards.front: A bearing is measured from which reference direction?

options.text: North.
options.explanation: Bearings always begin from the North line at the relevant starting point. The angle is then measured clockwise from North to the required direction.

options.text: East.
options.explanation: East corresponds to a bearing of 090°, but it is not the reference direction. Bearings are measured clockwise starting from North, which is 000°.

options.text: South.
options.explanation: South corresponds to a bearing of 180°, so it is a possible destination direction rather than the reference direction. Bearings start from North.

options.text: West.
options.explanation: West corresponds to a bearing of 270°, but bearings do not start there. Their reference direction is always North at the starting point.

cards.front: A bearing is measured clockwise or anticlockwise?

options.text: Clockwise.
options.explanation: By convention, a bearing is the angle turned clockwise from North to the required direction. This ensures that each direction has one standard three-figure bearing.

options.text: Anticlockwise.
options.explanation: Measuring anticlockwise would generally produce a different angle and is not the bearings convention. Bearings are measured clockwise from the North line.

options.text: Either direction.
options.explanation: A bearing uses one specified direction of rotation, rather than whichever direction gives the smaller angle. It must be measured clockwise from North.

options.text: The shortest direction.
options.explanation: Using the shortest direction can lead to an anticlockwise angle, which is not a standard bearing. The angle must always be measured clockwise from North.

cards.front: How many digits must a three-figure bearing have before °?

options.text: Three digits.
options.explanation: A three-figure bearing contains exactly three digits before the degree symbol. Leading zeros are added when necessary, such as writing 8° as 008°.

options.text: Two digits.
options.explanation: Using two digits omits a required leading zero for bearings below 100°. A three-figure bearing must contain exactly three digits before the degree symbol.

options.text: One digit.
options.explanation: A single digit gives an ordinary angle notation rather than a three-figure bearing. Leading zeros must be included to make exactly three digits.

options.text: Four digits.
options.explanation: Four digits would add an unnecessary leading zero and would no longer be a three-figure bearing. Exactly three digits must appear before the degree symbol.

cards.front: In the bearing of B from A, stand at [ ___ ] and look towards [ ___ ].
cards.back: In the bearing of B from A, stand at A and look towards B.

options.text: In the bearing of B from A, stand at A and look towards B.
options.explanation: The word “from” identifies the observation point, so the bearing of B from A is measured while standing at A and facing towards B.

options.text: In the bearing of B from A, stand at B and look towards A.
options.explanation: This reverses the starting point and destination, giving the bearing of A from B. For B from A, stand at A and look towards B.

options.text: In the bearing of B from A, stand at A and look towards A.
options.explanation: Looking towards the same point at which you are standing does not define the required direction. For B from A, stand at A and look towards B.

options.text: In the bearing of B from A, stand at B and look towards B.
options.explanation: Standing at B and looking towards B gives no direction between the two locations. The wording “B from A” requires standing at A and looking towards B.

cards.front: A bearing from A must use which North line?

options.text: The North line at A.
options.explanation: The phrase “from A” makes A the starting point of the bearing. Therefore, the clockwise angle must be measured from the North line drawn at A.

options.text: The North line at B.
options.explanation: Using the North line at B would measure an angle from the destination and could give the reverse bearing. A bearing from A uses North at A.

options.text: The South line at A.
options.explanation: Bearings are measured from North, not South, at the named starting point. Since the bearing is from A, the correct reference is North at A.

options.text: The North line at the midpoint.
options.explanation: The reference line must pass through the starting point, not a point between the locations. A bearing from A is measured from the North line at A.

cards.front: Write 8° as a three-figure bearing.

options.explanation: A three-figure bearing must have exactly three digits, so two leading zeros are placed before 8. The angle itself remains unchanged at 8°.
Placing the zero after 8 changes the value from 8° to 80°. Leading zeros must instead be added before the angle, giving 008°.
Adding zeros after the digit changes the angle to 800°, which is not the original direction. Two leading zeros produce the required bearing 008°.
This has only two digits before the degree symbol, so it is not a three-figure bearing. One more leading zero is required, giving 008°.

cards.front: As three-figure bearings, East is [ ___ ] and South is [ ___ ].
cards.back: As three-figure bearings, East is 090° and South is 180°.

options.text: As three-figure bearings, East is 090° and South is 180°.
options.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from North. East is a quarter-turn clockwise, giving 090°, while South is a half-turn clockwise, giving 180°.

options.text: As three-figure bearings, East is 180° and South is 090°.
options.explanation: This swaps the bearings for East and South. From North, East is 90° clockwise and South is 180° clockwise, so their bearings are 090° and 180° respectively.

options.text: As three-figure bearings, East is 270° and South is 180°.
options.explanation: The bearing 270° points West, not East. East is reached by turning 90° clockwise from North, so its three-figure bearing is 090°; South is 180°.

options.text: As three-figure bearings, East is 090° and South is 270°.
options.explanation: The bearing 270° points West, not South. South is a half-turn clockwise from North, so its bearing is 180°, while East is correctly represented by 090°.

cards.front: As three-figure bearings, North is [ ___ ] and West is [ ___ ].
cards.back: As three-figure bearings, North is 000° and West is 270°.

options.text: As three-figure bearings, North is 000° and West is 270°.
options.explanation: North is the starting direction for measuring bearings, so it is 000°. West is three-quarters of a full clockwise turn from North, which gives 270°.

options.text: As three-figure bearings, North is 090° and West is 270°.
options.explanation: The bearing 090° points East, not North. North is the zero direction and must be written as 000° in three-figure form; West is 270°.

options.text: As three-figure bearings, North is 000° and West is 090°.
options.explanation: The bearing 090° points East rather than West. Travelling clockwise from North to West requires three quarter-turns, so West has a bearing of 270°.

options.text: As three-figure bearings, North is 180° and West is 090°.
options.explanation: This confuses North with South and West with East. North is the starting direction at 000°, while West is 270° clockwise from North.

cards.front: What is the three-figure bearing of South-West?

options.explanation: South-West lies halfway between South at 180° and West at 270°. Adding 45° to 180° gives the three-figure bearing 225°.
The bearing 135° points South-East, showing that East and West have been confused. South-West lies between 180° and 270°, exactly halfway at 225°.
This uses an incorrect 35° offset from South. The eight principal compass directions are separated by 45°, so South-West is 180° + 45° = 225°.
The bearing 315° points North-West, not South-West. South-West is halfway between South at 180° and West at 270°, giving a bearing of 225°.

cards.front: A direction is 34° anticlockwise from North. What clockwise bearing is it?

options.explanation: A 34° anticlockwise turn from North is equivalent to a clockwise turn of the remainder of a full circle. Therefore, the bearing is 360° - 34° = 326°.
This treats an anticlockwise angle as though it were clockwise. Subtracting 34° from a full turn converts it correctly: 360° - 34° = 326°.
This results from subtracting 56° rather than the stated 34°. The equivalent clockwise bearing is found using 360° - 34°, which equals 326°.
This subtracts 24° from 360°, losing ten degrees from the given angle. The correct conversion is 360° - 34° = 326°.

cards.front: When drawing a bearing, where should the protractor centre be placed?

options.text: On the starting point.
options.explanation: A bearing describes the turn made at the starting point, so the protractor’s centre must be placed there. This allows the angle to be measured from North accurately.

options.text: On the destination point.
options.explanation: Placing the centre at the destination measures the reverse direction instead. The bearing begins at the starting point, so the protractor’s centre must be positioned there.

options.text: On the North arrow.
options.explanation: The North arrow shows the reference direction but is not necessarily the angle’s vertex. The protractor’s centre belongs on the starting point, where the bearing begins.

options.text: On the line midpoint.
options.explanation: The midpoint is not the vertex from which the direction is measured. Bearings are measured at the starting point, so the protractor’s centre must be placed there.

cards.front: When drawing a bearing, what should the protractor 0° line line up with?
cards.back: The North line at the starting point.

options.text: The North line at the starting point.
options.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from North, so the protractor’s 0° line must align with the North line drawn through the starting point.

options.text: The South line at the starting point.
options.explanation: Aligning with South introduces a 180° error because bearings use North as their reference direction. The 0° line must align with the North line at the starting point.

options.text: The travel line at the starting point.
options.explanation: The line of travel shows the final direction, not the zero reference. The protractor’s 0° line should align with North before the clockwise angle is marked.

options.text: The East line at the starting point.
options.explanation: Using East as zero shifts the measurement by 90°. Bearings always begin from North, so the protractor’s 0° line must align with the North line.

cards.front: If protractor numbers get smaller as you move clockwise from North, what is wrong?
cards.back: You are using the wrong scale.

options.text: You are using the wrong scale.
options.explanation: Bearing angles must increase as you move clockwise from North. If the numbers decrease, you are reading the protractor’s opposite scale and must switch scales.

options.text: You have misplaced the protractor centre.
options.explanation: A misplaced centre affects the angle’s vertex but does not determine whether the numbers increase clockwise. Decreasing numbers show that the wrong protractor scale is being read.

options.text: You have aligned with the East line.
options.explanation: Aligning with East would create a 90° offset, but it does not explain the decreasing numbers. That pattern means you are reading the wrong protractor scale.

options.text: You have marked the destination point.
options.explanation: Marking the destination does not control the order of the protractor numbers. If they decrease clockwise from North, the wrong scale is being used.

cards.front: To measure a bearing from a diagram, measure [ ___ ] from North to the [ ___ ].
cards.back: To measure a bearing from a diagram, measure clockwise from North to the line of travel.

options.text: To measure a bearing from a diagram, measure clockwise from North to the line of travel.
options.explanation: A bearing is defined as the clockwise angle measured from the North line at the starting point to the line showing the direction of travel.

options.text: To measure a bearing from a diagram, measure anticlockwise from North to the line of travel.
options.explanation: This uses the wrong direction of rotation. Bearings are always measured clockwise from North to the line of travel and are written using three figures.

options.text: To measure a bearing from a diagram, measure clockwise from North to the North line.
options.explanation: Measuring back to the North line would give zero rather than the required direction. The clockwise angle must finish at the line of travel.

options.text: To measure a bearing from a diagram, measure anticlockwise from North to the starting point.
options.explanation: This confuses both the rotation and the endpoint of the angle. A bearing is measured clockwise from North to the line of travel, with its vertex at the starting point.

cards.front: Reverse bearings differ by [ ___ ] because the opposite direction is a [ ___ ].
cards.back: Reverse bearings differ by 180° because the opposite direction is a half-turn.

options.text: Reverse bearings differ by 180° because the opposite direction is a half-turn.
options.explanation: A reverse bearing points in exactly the opposite direction. Opposite directions are separated by 180°, which is one half-turn around a point.

options.text: Reverse bearings differ by 90° because the opposite direction is a quarter-turn.
options.explanation: A 90° quarter-turn gives a perpendicular direction, not the opposite direction. Reverse bearings differ by 180° because changing direction is a half-turn.

options.text: Reverse bearings differ by 360° because the opposite direction is a full-turn.
options.explanation: A 360° full-turn returns to the original direction rather than reversing it. Reverse bearings differ by 180°, corresponding to a half-turn.

options.text: Reverse bearings differ by 180° because the opposite direction is a full-turn.
options.explanation: The angular difference of 180° is correct, but 180° is a half-turn, not a full-turn. A full-turn is 360° and returns to the original direction.

cards.front: To find a reverse bearing, what do you do if the bearing is less than 180°?

options.explanation: Adding 180° makes a half-turn to obtain the opposite direction. Since the original bearing is below 180°, the result remains below 360°.

options.text: Subtract 180°.
options.explanation: Subtracting 180° from a bearing below 180° produces a negative value. The reverse bearing is found by adding 180°, giving a valid three-figure bearing.

options.text: Add 90°.
options.explanation: Adding 90° produces a perpendicular direction, which is only a quarter-turn. A reverse bearing requires a half-turn, so 180° must be added.

options.text: Subtract 90°.
options.explanation: Subtracting 90° makes only a quarter-turn and may also produce a negative value. The opposite direction is reached by adding 180°.

cards.front: To find a reverse bearing, what do you do if the bearing is 180° or more?

options.text: Subtract 180°.
options.explanation: For a bearing of 180° or more, subtracting 180° gives the opposite direction while keeping the result within the standard bearing range from 000° to 360°.
Adding 180° produces a value of 360° or more, which is not immediately a standard bearing. Subtracting 180° gives the reverse bearing directly.

options.text: Subtract 90°.
options.explanation: Subtracting 90° changes the direction by only a quarter-turn. Reverse bearings point in opposite directions, so the required change is 180°.

options.text: Subtract 360°.
options.explanation: Subtracting 360° represents a full rotation and leaves the direction unchanged, often producing a negative representation. The reverse bearing is found by subtracting 180°.

cards.front: The bearing of B from A is 070°. What is the bearing of A from B?

options.explanation: Because 070° is less than 180°, add 180° to reverse the direction: 070° + 180° = 250°.
This comes from calculating 180° - 70°, which does not make a half-turn from the original bearing. Adding 180° gives the reverse bearing, 250°.
This uses 360° - 70°, which reflects the direction around the north line rather than reversing it. The reverse bearing is 070° + 180° = 250°.
Doubling 070° does not produce the opposite direction. A reverse bearing is found by changing the bearing by 180°, giving 250°.

cards.front: The bearing of D from C is 238°. What is the bearing of C from D?

options.explanation: Because 238° is at least 180°, subtract 180° to find the reverse bearing: 238° - 180° = 58°, written as the three-figure bearing 058°.
This comes from calculating 360° - 238°, which reflects the direction rather than reversing it. Subtracting 180° gives 058°.
Adding 180° gives 418°, which lies outside the standard bearing range and has not been normalised. Subtracting 180° directly gives the reverse bearing 058°.
This results from an arithmetic slip when subtracting 180° from 238°. The correct calculation is 238° - 180° = 58°, written 058°.

cards.front: When finding an angle at B, from which point must both directions be measured before subtracting?

options.text: From B.
options.explanation: Angle ABC has its vertex at B, so both directions must be considered from B. Their bearings can then be subtracted to find the angle at B.

options.text: From A.
options.explanation: Measuring both directions from A would describe an angle with vertex A, not angle ABC. Since B is the middle letter, both directions must be measured from B.

options.text: From C.
options.explanation: Measuring from C would find an angle with vertex C rather than B. For angle ABC, the middle letter identifies B as the common starting point.

options.text: From north.
options.explanation: Individual bearings are measured clockwise from north, but the two directions used for angle ABC must share B as their starting point before their bearings are subtracted.

cards.front: From A, B is on a bearing of 040°. What is the bearing of A from B?

options.explanation: The original bearing 040° is below 180°, so add 180° to reverse it: 040° + 180° = 220°.
This comes from calculating 180° - 40°, which does not turn the direction through 180°. The reverse bearing is 040° + 180° = 220°.
This uses 360° - 40°, reflecting the bearing about north instead of finding the opposite direction. Adding 180° gives 220°.
Doubling the original bearing does not create a reverse direction. Reverse bearings differ by exactly 180°, so the correct bearing is 220°.

cards.front: From B, BA has bearing 220° and BC has bearing 120°. What is angle ABC?

options.explanation: Both bearings are measured from B, so their difference gives the angle between BA and BC: 220° - 120° = 100°.
This is the reflex angle obtained from 360° - 100°. The smaller angle ABC is found directly from the bearing difference, 220° - 120° = 100°.
This comes from subtracting 220° from 360°, using only one bearing. The angle between the two directions is their difference, which is 100°.
Adding the bearings gives 340°, but bearings from a common point must be subtracted to find the angle between them. Their difference is 100°.
